verdict.reasoning: Patient reports diarrhea for three days and vomiting currently, but duration of vomiting is not stated as 3 days. Transcript: diarrhea started three days ago (“Three days ago now.”) and vomiting is described but without a 3‑day duration. Saying vomiting for 3 days adds duration not given.

Patient says, “It's very loose, but it started as being very watery” and “Today alone, I've been at least four times,” and also “I lost count,” supporting stools more than four times per day and initially watery then very loose.

Patient states, “I can't seem to be able to keep anything in me. Not even water, not even my tea, not even any liquid stuff. I've just been throwing up everything,” which supports vomiting everything including liquids.

Patient reports feeling hot: “Yes, I've been running at serious temperature. I'm literally boiling,” and also says, “No, because I've not got one” when asked about checking with a thermometer, matching feeling feverish without measured temperature.

Location and pattern are described: “It's kind of like towards my navel area... towards like, the center of my navel” and “When it comes, I feel the strong urge to go to the loo and then sort of releases me and sort of like, comes again,” supporting intermittent periumbilical pain associated with urge to defecate.
Patient notes, “my brother has actually been having similar symptoms for the past few days” and confirms contact: “So you've been in contact with him, have you?” / “Yes.”

She reports using ORS and no benefit: “I've tried the ORs… The salt, sugar mix… I've taken that like three times a day for the past two days” and later, “To be honest, they're not getting any better… I doubt that even that has had the chance to work.”

When asked about other medical or abdominal problems, patient replies, “Well, apart from the fact that this one is giving me abdominal pains. No previous abdominal pains before I get the odd, you know, menstrual cramps…,” indicating no other significant past medical/abdominal history mentioned.
Patient states, “I get the odd, you know, menstrual cramps and all that,” confirming a history of menstrual cramps.
In response to regular medications: “Well, I take my vitamins, Vitamin D every day. That's about all that I regularly take.”
Social/family context: “I live with my brother and my mum.” This fact reflects living situation, not explicit family disease history, but the statement itself is accurate.
Same quote supports this: “I live with my brother and my mum.”
Occupation and current work status: “I'm a graphics designer.” and “I'm working from home today because I can't,” indicating she is a graphics designer working from home due to illness.
Tobacco and alcohol: “Well, I don't smoke, but, you know, I have a pint from time to time,” supporting occasional alcohol use and non‑smoker status.
On drug use: Doctor asks, “And do you take any other drugs?” and patient replies, “No, like I said, I only take vitamins…,” indicating no (other) drug use, supporting no illicit drug use.

Fever description and lack of measurement: “Yes, I've been running at serious temperature. I'm literally boiling… to the touch, I'm like, literally roasting,” and “No, because I've not got one,” about not having a thermometer.

Urine timing and color: “When did you last pass urine, do you think?” / “At least an hour ago.” and about color: “To be honest, I can't know how to look, so I really couldn't see,” supporting last urine about an hour ago and unknown color.
Doctor’s assessment: “it sounds like it might be an infectious gastroenteritis that you've got,” which corresponds to acute gastroenteritis.

Symptoms noted in assessment: Doctor links her presentation (“because your brother's had a similar thing, it sounds like it might be an infectious gastroenteritis…”) and throughout the history she has diarrhea, vomiting, feeling feverish, and abdominal pain, which are used to support the diagnosis.

Etiology discussion: “which is usually caused by a virus, but it can be from something you've eate as well… I think it's probably important to get a sample of the stool so we can make sure that you haven't got a nasty bacterial infection which needs specific treatment,” indicating likely viral but possible bacterial cause.

Doctor says, “I think it's probably important to get a sample of the stool… we should see you so that we can check your hydration and get that sample sent off as soon as possible… we can make you an urgent appointment and then you can get the sample sent off and we can check your hydration,” which matches an urgent appointment for hydration assessment and stool sample.

Advice given: “you need to carry on with your rehydration salts and just have very small amounts… Keep drinking, keep going with the rehydration salts. Just tiny sips constantly so that your stomach doesn't get overfilled and you vomit,” which is continuation of ORS in small sips and monitoring hydration.

Dietary advice: “And just have very simple food. If you're going to have anything like two toast or biscuit or something really light like that. Avoid fruit, vegetables, milk, anything like that, which might just make it worse.”

Escalation plan: “if in the meantime you're feeling more unwell, then we would get you seen urgently in ae,” and patient hopes to avoid A&E, implying possible need for A&E if condition worsens or hydration fails.

Booking support: “So we can, we can make you an urgent appointment…” and later, “Okay, so you're happy to book an appointment through the support line?” / “Yes, please. Right. Okay. We'll do that for you,” confirming support to book an urgent clinic appointment.
